newsitem.title: UK: London marks ten year anniversary of Big Bang.
newsitem.headline: London marks ten year anniversary of Big Bang.

text.p: Luminaries from London's financial community gather on Wednesday on the long-deserted stock exchange floor to mark the ten-year anniversary of the "Big Bang" reforms which killed off floor trading in London.

Yet a decade after the radical reforms swept away years of share trading tradition in Europe's busiest stock market, major questions remain about the exchange's future direction -- making Big Bang seem an unfinished revolution to many in the market.

For next year the London Stock Exchange (LSE) plans a new share trading network where trades are automatically matched by computer, supplementing the current system where market makers set prices on screen but agree trades by phone.
But details of the new "order-driven" system are still being defined and it was accepted reluctantly by leading brokerages.
"It well be another big cultural shock if we go to an order driven system," said one senior trader, "it will be as big a change as Big Bang."

Under the deregulating British government of Margaret Thatcher, the Big Bang reforms abolished fixed commissions on share trades and ended the division between jobbers who traded stock and brokers who placed the orders.
Small on paper, the reforms of October 27 1986 changed the face of the London stock market.
They led to a wave of mergers to create the big integrated investment banks that dominate the London stock market today.

Meantime the introduction of the Seaq electronic share trading screen quickly killed off the old stock exchange trading floor, adding to the dramatic process that shaped careers and is etched into the memories of market players.
"What upset me and people of my era was that we were going to have to leave our stage and go sit behind screens," said Brian Winterflood, managing director of broking house Winterflood Securities.

"Getting up to go to that stock exchange in those days was like getting up to go to the theater for me. It was a wonderful place," said Winterflood, who joined the LSE in 1953. "Leaving the floor was a tragedy for me. But one adopts and adapts."
Robin Packer, a managing director of brokerage UBS, said he and many of his colleagues on the LSE floor feared electronic trading threatened their livelihood.

"There was this feeling that under the new system, there wouldn't be a role for us," Packer said. "There were a lot who fell to the wayside. But a lot of people got into sales trading, and that's a very important function in today's markets."
When reforms were first introduced a decade ago, the feeling among traders, jobbers and brokers was that firms were not given enough time to implement changes, said Packer.

"We had been given very little time to organize a new system. There was also the feeling that they were breaking up a system that was hugely efficient. "But at the end of the day, (the new system) was more efficient and international."

Indeed, the LSE fended off competiton from European bourses and remains Europe's busiest stock exchange. An unprecedented 646.3 billion pounds of UK and Irish stocks changed hands in 1995, a rise of 6.6 percent.

The LSE, criticised for dragging its feet in carrying out its current reforms, is this week expected to approve a more precise definition of the new order-driven market -- paving the way for the introduction of the service next summer.
The continuing revolution seems inevitable but some old hands believe something valuable has been lost in the past ten years of upheaval.
"The system had to change because it wasn't moving ahead fast enough to be in the international game," said Winterflood. "It was a place where my word was my bond. Now that's gone."
